title: Dim Sum Lunch in Phuket Old Town: A Guide to Yan Long
excerpt: Plan dim sum lunch at Yan Long with service-time guidance, har gow, sharing tips and a practical approach to ordering in rounds.

content:
A dim sum lunch in Phuket Old Town is a chance to slow down over small dishes, tea and conversation. At Yan Long, the official dining listing places dim sum service between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m., making it a lunch option rather than an early breakfast stop. Plan within that window, confirm availability when booking, and begin with a small selection that leaves room to try something else.

For a first visit, the aim is variety without a crowded table. Different textures and cooking methods usually make a more interesting meal than several baskets that all taste alike.

Plan lunch around the dim sum service

Phuket has a strong morning dim sum culture, but individual restaurants follow different schedules. Yan Long opens for lunch and dinner; that does not mean the dim sum selection is available throughout every service. Its official dining listing separates the dim sum hours from the restaurant's broader opening hours.

Arrive with enough time to order comfortably rather than aiming for the end of the window. If your group has a fixed departure, mention it in advance and ask what the kitchen recommends. A reservation request is also a sensible moment to check which dishes are available and whether any require advance notice.

Start with a dish you can understand

Har gow, also written ha gow, is a useful starting point. These shrimp dumplings have a delicate, translucent wrapper and a filling that lets the seafood take the lead. Yan Long lists them among its signature dishes. They offer a clear introduction to the pleasure of dim sum: a small item with a distinct texture, shape and flavour.

From there, ask for a contrasting preparation. A crisp item alongside a steamed one changes the rhythm of the meal. A different filling may make the next basket more worthwhile than simply ordering more of the first. Use the full menu at the table to make those choices rather than assuming every familiar dim sum dish is offered.

  • Choose one steamed dish as your starting point.
  • Add a different texture or filling from the available selection.
  • Check how many pieces are in each serving before sharing.
  • Pause after the first round and decide what the table still wants.

Order in rounds, with the whole table in mind

Small plates can make it surprisingly easy to overorder. Before adding another basket, think about who is actually eating it. A table of four does not necessarily need four portions of everything, but one basket may leave somebody without a taste. Piece counts matter more than the number of dish names on the order.

A useful first round gives everyone something familiar and something to explore. Let the quieter diners choose too. Children, guests with smaller appetites and people avoiding particular ingredients may want different things from the most enthusiastic eater at the table.

Once the first dishes arrive, you can judge appetite more accurately. This also gives you a chance to repeat a favourite without committing to a large spread before anyone has tasted anything. Ask the team about practical ordering times if you intend to add another round near the end of dim sum service.

Give tea a place at lunch

Tea is part of the pleasure of a dim sum meal, but you do not need specialist knowledge to choose it. Describe the flavour you enjoy: light and fragrant, fuller and more roasted, or something familiar. Ask which Chinese teas are currently offered and whether they are served by the pot or another arrangement.

Taste a dumpling before adding a strong sauce. Then use a little seasoning if you want it. Tea, a sip of water and a change of dish can make subtle flavours easier to notice than covering everything with the same condiment.

If anyone is sensitive to caffeine, check the available alternatives. Avoid treating a tea name as a health promise; choose it for the flavour and the kind of lunch you want.

Decide whether this is a dim sum meal or a larger lunch

A few baskets may be the entire meal for a light eater, while another table may want to continue with a shared main dish. Decide which kind of lunch you are planning before ordering a full second course.

Lunch styleA useful approach
A light stopBegin with a modest range of dim sum and reassess appetite.
A relaxed shared mealVary fillings and textures, adding another round if wanted.
A signature-dish lunchKeep the dim sum opening smaller and plan the main dish first.

If Peking duck is also on your list, read our guide to planning a duck-led meal. For a wider introduction, the signature-dish guide helps distinguish the roles different dishes can play.

Make the visit easy for your group

Yan Long is on the first floor of Royal Phuket City Hotel on Phang-Nga Road. Include the restaurant name when arranging your arrival, and leave enough time to reach your table. Larger parties should discuss seating and any private-room requirements before the day.

Tell the restaurant about allergies when booking and repeat them when ordering. A dumpling's appearance does not reveal every ingredient in its wrapper, filling or sauce. Ask specifically about what needs to be avoided; do not assume that a vegetable-looking item is vegetarian or that a translucent wrapper is gluten-free.

Quick lunch questions

Can I have dim sum for dinner?

The official listing gives a daytime dim sum window. Check directly if you want a particular item outside those hours; the restaurant's dinner opening time is not confirmation of dim sum availability.

Do I need to know the dish names?

No. Describe what you enjoy and ask for guidance on the current menu. Filling, texture and cooking method are often more helpful than trying to remember a name.

What is the next step?

Request a lunch table, mentioning your group size and any dietary needs. A few carefully chosen baskets, enough time to enjoy them and room for conversation are a good starting point.
